claims.text: In-situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction with environmental control can simultaneously monitor oxidation behaviour and phase stability under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
CrCoFeMnNi is an example of a high-entropy alloy suitable for the proposed method.
The starting CrCoFeMnNi alloy is homogenized and in a single-phase solid-solution state.
In-situ HT-XRD can be applied while heating an alloy under an oxidizing atmosphere.
A temperature range from 750 °C to 1320 °C is appropriate for the proposed measurements.
The oxidizing gas atmosphere can be controlled to mimic service conditions.
Real-time evolution of XRD peaks can indicate oxide formation and phase transformation of the parent alloy.
During continuous heating, in-situ HT-XRD captures time-dependent peak shifts and the emergence or disappearance of diffraction peaks.
Time-dependent diffraction changes correlate with oxidation progression and phase transitions.
The appearance of oxide peaks or shifts associated with structural transformations will reveal oxidation behaviour and phase stability.
Diffraction-pattern changes alone will correlate quantitatively with oxidation kinetics.
Separate ex-situ methods provide only discrete snapshots and lack real-time correlation between oxidation and phase transformations.
Signal resolution at extreme temperatures may limit the effectiveness of in-situ HT-XRD.
Overlapping diffraction features from transient phases or minor oxides may limit phase identification.
Qualitative phase changes are expected to be detectable by in-situ HT-XRD.
Instrumental resolution may prevent precise quantification of oxidation kinetics and the onset times of minor phase events.
Simultaneous mass-gain measurements can provide an independent measure of oxidation kinetics.
Failure to detect diffraction changes despite independently detectable oxidation would falsify the proposed capability of HT-XRD.
